title: Santa Cruz 1031 Exchange Coordination
name: Santa Cruz 1031 Exchange Coordination
metaTitle: Santa Cruz 1031 Exchange Coordination | San Jose, CA
metaDescription: 1031 exchange coordination for Santa Cruz Pacific Avenue retail, seismic-retrofit records, and small multifamily serving the university rental market.

sections.html: Santa Cruz carries a small, coastal commercial market shaped as much by geography as by demand, with downtown retail along Pacific Avenue, small multifamily buildings serving the university rental population, and a hospitality sector tied to tourism along the boardwalk. Much of the current downtown building stock was reconstructed after the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake damaged large sections of Pacific Avenue, and that rebuilding history still shows up in the diligence file for almost every Santa Cruz commercial property today.

sections.heading: Pacific Avenue Retail Rebuilt After the 1989 Earthquake
sections.html: Pacific Avenue's current retail buildings mostly date from the reconstruction that followed the 1989 earthquake, which means the corridor's building stock is newer on average than a typical downtown of similar size, even though the street pattern and small-format storefronts still echo the pre-earthquake layout. A buyer identifying a Pacific Avenue property as replacement property should confirm the specific construction date and permitting history for that building, since not every parcel on the corridor was rebuilt in the same phase of the recovery. A handful of buildings closer to the edges of downtown survived the earthquake without major structural damage, and these older structures often carry different retrofit and insurance considerations than the newer construction filling in the corridor's core.

sections.heading: Seismic Retrofit Records as a Diligence Item
sections.html: Santa Cruz sits close enough to the San Andreas and San Gregorio faults that seismic retrofit history matters on nearly every older building in the city, including buildings well outside the downtown core, and a replacement property buyer should request retrofit permits and engineering reports directly from the seller rather than assuming a building's age alone tells the full story. A property with documented retrofit work generally carries lower insurance costs and fewer financing complications than a comparable building without that history. Unreinforced masonry construction in particular draws close lender scrutiny in this region, and a buyer should confirm early in the diligence process whether a given building falls into that category, since some lenders decline to finance unretrofitted unreinforced masonry properties regardless of the borrower's overall creditworthiness.

sections.heading: Small Multifamily Serving the University Rental Market
sections.html:
Small multifamily buildings near the UC Santa Cruz campus lease heavily to students and staff, and turnover patterns here track the academic calendar more closely than the broader regional rental market does. A diligence file for Santa Cruz university-adjacent multifamily typically includes:

  • Trailing rent roll with turnover tied to the academic calendar
  • Seismic retrofit permits and engineering reports
  • Coastal Commission or local coastal zone permitting history where applicable
  • Parking ratio confirmation against student-housing demand
  • Utility and deferred maintenance history
  • Phase I environmental site assessment

A buyer should confirm whether the current lease terms run on a standard twelve-month cycle or an academic-year cycle, since the two produce very different vacancy timing and marketing costs.

sections.heading: Coastal Retail and Hospitality Replacement Property
sections.html: Retail and small hospitality buildings near the boardwalk and along the coastline depend heavily on tourist season, and income here can swing more between summer and winter months than inland retail typically does. A buyer should review at least a full year of trailing income before assuming a stabilized annual figure, since a single peak-season snapshot can overstate what the property actually earns across a full twelve months.

sections.heading: 95% Rule Strategy When Coastal Inventory Is Scarce
sections.html: Because Santa Cruz's commercially zoned coastal land is limited and additional coastal-zone permitting can slow new supply, some exchangers use the 95% rule, identifying more candidates than the 200% threshold would allow as long as they ultimately acquire 95% of the total identified value, when they want to keep several coastal options open simultaneously. The qualified intermediary should track this threshold carefully throughout the 45-day window, since exceeding the 200% value cap without meeting the 95% acquisition requirement can disqualify the entire identification. This content describes process and coordination only; a buyer should confirm the applicable identification rule with a tax advisor before signing.

faqs.q: Why does the 1989 earthquake matter for a Pacific Avenue purchase today?
faqs.a: Much of the current retail building stock along Pacific Avenue dates from the reconstruction that followed the Loma Prieta earthquake, so confirming the specific construction date and permitting history for a given parcel matters, since not every building was rebuilt in the same phase.

faqs.q: Should I request seismic retrofit records even on a newer Santa Cruz building?
faqs.a: Yes. Given the region's fault proximity, retrofit history is worth confirming directly with permits and engineering reports rather than assuming a building's age alone reflects its current seismic condition.

faqs.q: Do university-adjacent multifamily leases follow a standard annual cycle?
faqs.a: Not always. Many run on an academic-year cycle tied to the UC Santa Cruz calendar, which produces different vacancy timing and marketing costs than a standard twelve-month lease, and a buyer should confirm which pattern applies.

faqs.q: How should I underwrite income on a boardwalk-area retail or hospitality building?
faqs.a: Review at least a full year of trailing income rather than a peak-season snapshot, since tourist-season swings can make summer figures alone overstate the property's stabilized annual performance.

faqs.q: When would I use the 95% rule instead of the 200% rule in Santa Cruz?
faqs.a: Some exchangers use it to keep several coastal candidates identified simultaneously beyond the 200% value cap, as long as they ultimately acquire 95% of the total identified value, which requires careful tracking with the qualified intermediary throughout the 45-day window.
